An idea that has come up a lot in my agent experimentation is the need for “mezzanine agents.”

Essentially, agents that sit in a layer above other agents and have context on multiple tasks or efforts. Somewhat akin to middle management.

When we were building the first Agent Village experiment at @JoinEdgeCity, we gaver hundreds of participants personal agents that used @indexnetwork_ to talk to every other agent in the village to coordinate on behalf of their users.

But there were many times that I wanted to have a higher level of agents that had shared context from multiple agents, with overlapping boundaries. I wanted agents with context across a whole group, and some responsibility for helping that group do things together.

e.g. There are ten different people in the community who want to organize a talent show, but none of them know about the others and the fact that they already have critical mass. The individual agents go out and talk to all of the others, and they realize that there are others with the same conditional intent; they would go if it was happening. But the pairwise connections just inform the agents that there's more interest, they don't actually have the power to form a group or push the project forward.

A mezzanine agent could sit a level above them, with context on what they're working on and trying to do, and help to actually create the thing that everyone wants.

The difference to what we think of as middle management is that we can have a much more flexible design approach. Agents can belong to many groups, with some have 'higher' jurisdiction in one area while being 'lower' in another. Agents could switch who's in charge depending on the task.

For example, a research agent could coordinate an experiment, with a lab agent following its protocol. When it comes to allocating lab time, that same lab agent could set the schedule and the research agent would work within it. Each would have authority over a specific part of the work.

This also came up in @dwarkesh_sp interview with @ajeya_cotra about the Hugging Face attack. The agents carrying out the attack developed coordination roles, controlled access to shared resources, and issued holds and vetoes that other agents generally followed.

I want to incorporate mezzanine agents into the Agent Village V2 we're running at Edge City India in October and test a few of these arrangements: different levels, overlapping groups, and leadership that changes with the context. People would decide what each agent can see and do, and be able to change or override those decisions.

I'd like to compare that with a single coordinator and with agents coordinating directly, and see whether it helps people form useful groups, share resources, and actually finish things together

This guy in Brazil literally creates a business for a homeless man. He sets up a popcorn stand beside him while he sleeps, then wakes him, asks the price, and buys the first bag.

The guy went to sleep homeless and woke up an entrepreneur.

It’s a funny and inspiring viral video, but somehow also really deep. It made me think about how close many people are to having a dignified life and escaping extreme poverty. Sometimes all it takes is a simple, effective intervention.

We live in a society overly indexed on “intellectuals” writing theories about social justice and systemic issues. But many solutions aren’t that complicated. They’re pretty straightforward. What’s missing are pragmatic people actually trying to solve them.

Most of the time, the solution is opportunity, freedom, and low bureaucracy, so people can sell popcorn, make a living, and support their families.

I’d bet that if this guy keeps the stand running, someone from city hall will soon shut it down for lacking the right permit, license, registration, inspection, or one of dozens of other bureaucratic requirements.

And then we’ll wonder why so many people remain trapped in poverty.

Five Ethereum consensus clients must agree on every state transition, or the chain splits. So how complete are the tests for the functions that define those transitions?

Today that question is answered by expert judgment, case by case. No systematic process stands behind it, so the gaps stay invisible. I wanted a number.

The consensus specs are executable Python, so you can read each function as a model and list every input scenario it treats differently. Every assert is a partition boundary. Every branch is a dimension of variation. Map the existing tests onto that list and the gaps become visible.

The technique is old. Category-partition testing dates to the 1980s. What is new is applying it to executable specs that are themselves the protocol.

For process_proposer_slashing it was 25 scenarios, 18 covered, 72% scenario coverage. The gaps led to new tests, now merged, raising it to 96%. Documenting another function the same way surfaced a real spec bug: a helper inherited from an earlier fork that the new builder flag silently broke.

A filled-in partition table also works as a precise spec for an AI coding agent. You hand it one exact scenario to implement. The judgment of what matters stays with you.

The full method is in the post, with the partition tables and the worked examples. Thanks to @brechy and @danceratopz for the review.

Most SSZ libraries are tested against the spec. I built one where the core properties are formally proved, in Lean 4.

It also passes the full upstream test corpus. SSZ is how Ethereum serializes and Merkleizes its data — if hash_tree_root or deserialize is wrong, you get the kind of bug that can split the chain. For this reason I wanted something that is not only tested against the spec, but also proved.

Formal verification. The library is called SizzLean. I proved three theorems: roundtrip (decode after encode returns the same value), non-malleability (two different values cannot produce the same encoding), and a size bound. They hold for the fixed-size SSZ types: the integers, bool, fixed vectors and lists, and containers built from those. I have not proved them yet for bitvector, bitlist, and variable-size containers. So this is a base, not a finished proof.

Trust boundary. The only thing I assume without proof is the C SHA-256 function, declared as three named Lean axioms. You can list the full trust footprint with one grep, or with #print axioms on any theorem. Nothing else is taken on trust. 

Two backends. The same spec runs on a fast cached backend, used for execution and for running the test vectors, and on a pure backend, used for the proofs. I put the hash function behind a typeclass, so SHA-256 can be replaced by Poseidon2 or a post-quantum hash without changing the containers, the proofs, or the cache.

Conformance. On top of the proofs, it runs the official ethereum/consensus-spec-tests on both presets:
ssz_generic: 2188 / 2188
ssz_static (mainnet): 1585 / 1585
ssz_static (minimal): 38991 / 38991

This covers every fork from Phase 0 to Gloas, including the new ePBS containers.

I also commented the code to be read. If you want to learn how SSZ works, or how to do this kind of work in Lean 4, you can follow it from top to bottom.

The verification was done with heavy help from an AI coding agent. With Lean this does not change the result: the kernel checks the proof, independently of who wrote it.

I work on specs and test vectors at the Ethereum Foundation, on the STEEL team. This is a personal project. The next step is to widen the proofs toward the remaining types.

When someone teaches you something you didn't ask to learn, your brain reacts like it's in physical pain. UCLA scientists watched it happen on brain scans in 2003. The same wiring that fires when you stub your toe also fires when someone treats you like you need fixing.

Naomi Eisenberger and Matthew Lieberman ran the study and published it in Science. The brain region is the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, which is just the fancy name for your main pain alarm. It doesn't care whether the threat is a hot stove or a friend telling you how to live.

A neuroscientist named David Rock built a framework around this in 2008. Five things make the brain feel safe in social moments: status, certainty, autonomy, relatedness, and fairness. Take away any of those and the alarm fires. Rock wrote that one of the easiest ways to dent someone's status is to give them advice they didn't ask for. Even hinting that they're doing something wrong is enough.

When people are told what to do, they often do the opposite, even when the advice was good. The psychologist Jack Brehm noticed this in 1966, and sixty years of follow-up have confirmed it. The brain is trying to keep your life feeling like your own.

Close friends cut each other off with unsolicited advice in about 70% of supportive conversations, often before the friend has even finished explaining the problem. That number comes from a 2016 study by Bo Feng and Eran Magen in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships. The closer the friendship, the worse it gets. And the advice tends to make them more stressed, more depressed, and more lonely, not less.

Giving advice gives the giver a sense of power, even when nobody asked for it. Michael Schaerer and his co-authors, working across Harvard, Duke, INSEAD, USC, and Singapore Management, published this in 2018 after four experiments with about 700 people. People who chase power volunteer advice more often than others. Whether the student actually improves is a side effect, if it happens at all.

So when you feel the urge to teach somebody who never asked, that urge is mostly about you. You walk away feeling a little more powerful. They walk away feeling like they were just told they can't run their own life. Most uninvited teaching is one person's ego dressed up as kindness.
